Program Name: North American Center for Saffron Research and Development
Location: UVM BioResearch Complex, 661 Spear Street, South Burlington, VT 05405
Description: Farmers increasingly use high tunnels (unheated hoop houses) to grow crops that wouldn't normally survive local winters, extending their growing season. Since many growers already compete to sell the same popular crops, like early tomatoes and winter greens, the Norht American Center for Saffron Research and Development looked into a more unique and profitable option: saffron. Saffron is the world's most expensive spice, worth about $5,000 per pound, and comes from a fall-blooming crocus flower. It's also valued for health benefits, including fighting inflammation, possibly easing depression, and lowering cholesterol. The U.S. imported over 25 tons of it in 2013, showing there's real demand. Saffron can survive Vermont winters but doesn't grow well outdoors here, so in 2015 we tested growing it in milk crates and raised beds inside a high tunnel. The results were excellent: the yield beat those of top saffron-producing regions like Spain, and at Vermont's retail price of $19 per gram, that yield could be worth about $100,000 per acre. Compared to other high-tunnel crops, saffron was also more profitable per square foot, generating an estimated $4.03 in net revenue, versus $3.51 for tomatoes and $1.81 for winter greens. It also tested the saffron's quality and found it matched saffron from major producers like Iran, Spain, and Italy. This project has drawn a lot of attention from farmers and the media, and it is now being studied whether this method works long-term and whether there's a strong enough market to make saffron a viable crop for Vermont growers.
